incidents.cause: The pilot's failure to maintain clearance between his external load and trees while maneuvering.  Contributing to the accident were hilly terrain and trees.
The pilot's failure to maintain main rotor clearance from a fiber line while picking up a lineman.
The fatigue failure of the engine-to-transmission driveshaft adapter attachment bolt due to the application of inadequate torque on the bolt during assembly.
The student pilot's inadequate directional control during takeoff.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll, which resulted in a runway excursion and impact with terrain.
The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from a light pole while taxiing.

The student pilot's inadequate flare and the flight instructor's delayed remedial action and failure to maintain control of the airplane during a go-around. Contributing to the accident was the flight instructor's improper go-around procedures.
A loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination did not reveal any anomalies that would have precluded normal operation.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing flare.
The failure of the pilot of another airplane to maintain adequate visual lookout during the approach.
An in-flight collision with a bird.
An encounter with wind gusts, which resulted in a loss of control and a collapse of the nose landing gear.

The pilot's distraction while retrieving an item behind him while the helicopter was on the ground with the engine running, which led to his aggressive overapplication of the flight controls after experiencing a ground resonance condition and subsequent loss of helicopter control.
The pilot's failure to maintain adequate main rotor rpm during an autorotation, which resulted in a hard landing.
The pilot's improper use of the collective while landing, which resulted in an unrecoverable forward pitching moment. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's improper decision not to go-around.
The pilot's decision to exit the helicopter with the engine and rotors turning and the selection of unsuitable terrain for a landing, which resulted in a roll over.

The failure of water to properly drain through the fuselage drain holes, thus becoming trapped and freezing around the flight control cables, which resulted in the loss of control authority to the airplane's ailerons, elevator, and rudder.

The captain's failure to maintain directional control during landing with one engine inoperative. The failure of maintenance personnel to properly torque the elevator attachment hardware in accordance with the maintenance manual, which led to the detachment of the elevator. The failure of the nose landing gear steering manifold during landing, which resulted in an uncommanded and uncontrollable right turn, and the overhaul facility’s improper overhaul of the nose landing gear steering manifold.
Improper repair of a crack by maintenance personnel, which resulted in a subsequent failure of the glider canopy.

The tow plane pilot's loss of airplane control for reasons that could not be determined based on the available evidence. The pilot’s improper landing flare and subsequent improper recovery from a hard, bounced landing.
